title: Upcoding and Downcoding

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define upcoding (reporting a higher level of service than the documentation supports) and downcoding (reporting a lower level than documented).
- Explain why both upcoding and downcoding are compliance problems that make claims inaccurate.
- Select codes accurately by matching the reported code to the documentation in the medical record.
- Identify the medical office assistant's role in supporting accurate coding and escalating discrepancies rather than changing codes independently.
- Recognize common patterns of upcoding and downcoding, including cloned notes, added diagnoses, and payment-driven code changes.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Upcoding is like telling the store you bought a large drink when you really bought a small one, so the bill is bigger than it should be.

### Question 2

Downcoding is like telling the store you bought a small drink when you really bought a large one, so the bill is smaller than it should be.

### Question 3

Compliance is about telling the truth on the bill. Making the bill too big or too small are both ways of telling it wrong.

### Question 4

The note says 'small,' but the bill says 'extra large.' That is upcoding.

### Question 5

The note says 'extra large,' but the bill says 'small.' That is downcoding.

### Question 6

Accurate coding is like writing down exactly what you actually did, not what would earn the most or least money.

### Question 7

You can only say you did something if your notes actually show you did it.

### Question 8

The bill has to match what actually happened in this visit, not what might have happened.

### Question 9

The notes are the receipt of what happened; the code must match the notes.

### Question 10

Medically necessary means a doctor could honestly say, 'This patient really needs this.'

### Question 11

The person in charge of the care is the one who has to stand behind the bill.

### Question 12

An error is an accident; fraud is a lie on purpose. Both need fixing, but a lie on purpose is a much bigger deal.

### Question 13

It's only 'fraud' if the person knew they were lying; if it was an accident, it's just an error.

### Question 14

If you're overpaid by mistake, you have to give the extra money back; keeping it makes the problem worse.

### Question 15

The notes show a big job was done, but the bill claims a small one; the two no longer tell the same story.

### Question 16

The payer reads the codes and diagnoses on the bill and checks that the notes back them up.

### Question 17

If lots of bills are wrong, the big picture the health system sees is wrong too.

### Question 18

You don't pick the price tag first and then invent the work; the work comes first.

### Question 19

If your notes don't prove the big job, you can only bill the small one you can prove.

### Question 20

The assistant's job is to catch mistakes and pass them up the chain, not to make the final coding calls.

### Question 21

The code is a label for the work that was done, like a tag on a product.

### Question 22

Hiding by telling a smaller lie is still telling a lie.

### Question 23

Even if you're trying to be kind, you can't write a bigger bill than the work that was done.

### Question 24

No matter what, the bill has to tell the truth about the work.

### Question 25

The compliance program is like a safety net that catches billing mistakes before they become big problems.

### Question 26

The note says the visit was small, but the bill claims it was huge; that's upcoding.

### Question 27

The note says the visit was big, but the bill claims it was tiny; that's downcoding.

### Question 28

The level is decided by what the note shows was done and thought about, not by who the patient is.

### Question 29

Copying the same note for everyone is like giving every student the same report card; it doesn't show what actually happened.

### Question 30

Copying an old note is like copying last week's homework answers; they might not match today's lesson.

### Question 31

Making up a label that isn't in the notes to get a bigger bill is cheating, not clerical work.

### Question 32

Unbundling is like selling a burger as a bun and a patty separately to charge more than the combo price.

### Question 33

There's a specific law about lying on government bills, and upcoding can fall under it.

### Question 34

If the cashier hands you too much change, you give it back; the same is true when a payer overpays the office.

### Question 35

The bill still has to be honest even when the honesty would mean charging less.

### Question 36

Two wrong bills don't add up to one right bill.

### Question 37

When you see something wrong, tell the person in charge; don't quietly 'fix' it yourself.

### Question 38

Even if a boss asks, you don't write a dishonest bill; you tell someone who can fix it the right way.

### Question 39

The bill has to match the notes, even when someone wants to be nice about the price.

### Question 40

When two sets of rules disagree, follow the official rulebook, not whoever is loudest.

### Question 41

If the notes are fuzzy, ask the person who wrote them to make them clear; don't fill in the blanks yourself.

### Question 42

You can't change the notes after the fact to make the bill look better; the notes are supposed to be the real story.

### Question 43

Only the official notes for that visit count as proof of what happened.

### Question 44

When in doubt, don't hit send; check with the person who can clear it up first.

### Question 45

A brand-new customer and a returning customer get different paperwork; the bill has to reflect which one they are.

### Question 46

Time only counts toward the bill when the rules say it can and the note shows it.

### Question 47

A modifier is a little note on the bill that explains a special situation; it doesn't change the real size of the job.

### Question 48

If your homework is done right, a spot-check is no big deal.

### Question 49

If the records say a patient has serious health needs but the codes leave them out, the health system thinks everyone is healthier than they are.

### Question 50

It's fine to bill the biggest job you can prove; it's not fine to bill a bigger job than you can prove.

### Question 51

The bill follows the work, not the wallet.

### Question 52

You can't charge more just because the customer has a fancier wallet.

### Question 53

Even when you want to be generous, the bill still has to match the work that was done.

### Question 54

If it's not in the notes, it can't be on the bill.

### Question 55

You can't turn one job into two bills by changing the dates.

### Question 56

If the honest price is the honest price, you stick with it even if you wished it were higher.

### Question 57

If you speak up honestly about a problem, the rules are supposed to keep you safe for doing so.

### Question 58

The assistant can be the careful checker who says, 'Wait, this doesn't match the notes.'

### Question 59

Upcoding and over-coding are two names for the same 'too big' bill.

### Question 60

Downcoding and under-coding are two names for the same 'too small' bill.

### Question 61

A trained code expert reads the notes and picks the codes, with the provider in charge.

### Question 62

The auditor checks the bill against the notes; too big or too small are both 'not matching.'

### Question 63

The notes have to be real, signed, dated, and actually about that visit.

### Question 64

Medical decision-making is the 'how hard was the thinking' part of the visit.

### Question 65

The level comes from what the note shows was asked, checked, and thought about.

### Question 66

Spot a mismatch? Pass it up the chain so the right person fixes it.

### Question 67

A mistake is still a mistake; you fix it even though it wasn't on purpose.

### Question 68

If the proof only covers a level 2 job, even a level 3 bill is still too big.

### Question 69

If the notes only prove a level 2 job, level 2 is the only honest bill.

### Question 70

Billing too little is still a wrong bill, even though it's a 'too little' wrong.

### Question 71

If every single bill is 'extra large' no matter what happened, something is off and needs a closer look.

### Question 72

Even from the boss, a dishonest bill isn't okay; explain the problem and pass it to the right person.

### Question 73

If you knowingly help tell a lie on a bill, you can get in trouble too, not just the person who asked.

### Question 74

There's a legal path where a person who reports billing lies can help the government and even share in the money recovered.

### Question 75

Being scared of getting in trouble doesn't let you write a wrong bill; you still have to be accurate.

### Question 76

The practice signs a promise to bill honestly, and billing too little breaks that promise too.

### Question 77

These guidelines are the rulebook that says how much proof you need for each size of bill.

### Question 78

A big bill that you can fully prove is a fair bill, not a cheat.

### Question 79

If the proof shows level 2 and the bill says level 4, the bill is two steps too big.

### Question 80

Small amounts of everything add up to a small bill, not a big one.

### Question 81

Leaving real health problems off the record makes the system think everyone is doing better than they are.

### Question 82

A modifier is a footnote, not a magic wand that turns a small job into a big one.

### Question 83

Claim edits are like a spell-checker for bills that catches mistakes before they're mailed.

### Question 84

A good compliance program checks the work regularly and teaches everyone the right way.

### Question 85

When a spoken request clashes with the written rulebook, follow the rulebook and ask a manager to sort it out.
